main.text: It is proved that תנשמת thinsemeth is the little owl.

The word תנשמת thinsemeth is highly ambiguous among the Hebrews. For in Lev 11:30 it is [col. 286] among the species of lizards, as was said in its place. But in the eighteenth verse of the same chapter, with which we are dealing, it is a kind of unclean bird. The Greeks explain it as πορφυρίωνα [porphyriōna], a water bird in Libya and Commagene in Syria, so called from the colour of its beak and feet, for its feathers are blue ^{R1}. Jerome here has swan. Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] has אותיא otja, that is, otus, as I at least think: a bird very different in nature from the bustard (otis), although close to it in name. For the otus is a nocturnal bird, about which the Philosopher writes thus in book 8, chapter 12: Ὁ δὲ ὠτὸς, ὅμοιος ταῖς γλαυξὶ, καὶ περὶ τὰ ὦτα πτερύγια ἔχων. ἔνιοι δὲ αὐτὸν νυκτικόρακα καλοῦσιν. ἔστι δὲ κόβαλος, καὶ μιμητὴς, καὶ ἀντορχούμενος ἁλίσκεται, περιελθόντος θατέρου τῶν θηρευτῶν, καθάπερ γλαύξ. [Ho de ōtos, homoios tais glauxi, kai peri ta ōta pterygia echōn. enioi de auton nyktikoraka kalousin. esti de kobalos, kai mimētēs, kai antorchoumenos halisketai, perielthontos thaterou tōn thēreutōn, kathaper glaux.] “The otus is similar to little owls, and has little feathers around its ears” (hence its name). “Some call it the night raven. It is a buffoon and a mimic. And while it dances in turn opposite one of the fowlers who is dancing, it is caught by the other, who goes round it, like the little owl” ^{R2}. Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] has בותא bautha, or bavetha, also a kind of nocturnal bird, which in Greek is called βύας [byas], in Latin bubo [eagle owl], and in Arabic البوه [al-būh] albuho, from its cry. Yet even among the Arabs it is hardly agreed what البوه [al-būh] albuho properly is. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: البوه طاير يشبه البوم الا انه اصغر منه والانثي بوهة ويشبه بها الرجل الاحمق [al-būh ṭāyir yushbih al-būm illā annahu aṣghar minhu wa-l-unthī būha wa-yushabbah bihā al-rajul al-aḥmaq]: “Albuho is a bird similar to album, that is, to the eagle owl, except that it is smaller. The feminine is albuha. A man who is stupid is compared to it.” After proving this by an example taken from a certain poet, he adds: وقيل البوه ذكر البوم وقيل البوه اكبر من البوم [wa-qīla al-būh dhakar al-būm wa-qīla al-būh akbar min al-būm]: “By some albuho is said to be the male of album, and again by others to be larger than album,” that is, the eagle owl. Which is most true. For البوه [al-būh] albuho is certainly the Greek βύας [byas], that is, bubo, the largest of the nocturnal birds. Nor is the Chaldee בותא anything else; it is formed, after the manner of the language, from בוא, as עותא, iniquity, from עוא, and כותא, window, from כוא.

[III, 32] It is now worth knowing why the Syriac renders the Hebrew תנשמת as ܟܘܟܒܝ [כוכבי] cocabi, which at first sight will seem to mean ἀστερίαν [asterian], starry, because ܟܘܟܒ [כוכב] cocab is ἄστρον [astron], star; and the name ἀστερίας [asterias] is common to many birds. For sometimes it is an epithet of the larger eagle, which others call chrysaëtos. Aelian, History of Animals, book 2, chapter 39, [col. 287] Ἀκούω δέ τι καὶ γένος αἰετῶν, καὶ ὄνομα αὐτῶν χρυσαίετον ἔθεντο· ἄλλοι δὲ ἀςερίαν τὸν αὐτὸν καλοῦσιν [Akouō de ti kai genos aietōn, kai onoma autōn chrysaieton ethento; alloi de asterian ton auton kalousin]. So also Michael Apostolius, Century 2, Proverb 6. Sometimes it is a kind of hawk. Thus in Aristotle, History of Animals, book 9, chapter 36, among the species of hawks, after the buteo, the aesalon and the circus, the fourth is reckoned ὁ ἀςερίας [ho asterias]. It is also among the kinds of heron. Aristotle, book 9, chapter 11: Τῶν δ᾽ ἐρωδιῶν ἐςὶ τρία γένη· ὅτε πέλλος, καὶ ὁ λευκὸς, καὶ ὁ ἀςερίας καλούμενος [Tōn d’ erōdiōn esti tria genē; ho te pellos, kai ho leukos, kai ho asterias kaloumenos]. Hence Pliny, book 10, chapter 60: “Of little herons there are three kinds, the leucon, the asterias, the pellos.” Aelian too, History of Animals, book 5, chapter 36, which begins thus: Ὄνομά ἐςιν ὄρνιθος ἀςερίας [Onoma estin ornithos asterias], etc. There are therefore several birds of this name. Indeed, all birds that are painted and marked with spots like stars are called asteriae, or starry. Accordingly, since asterias is an epithet of many birds, it will be difficult to determine which one in particular the Syriac designates by the word ܟܘܟܒܝ [כוכבי] cocabi, if indeed it means starry. What of the fact that ܟܘܟܒܝ [כוכבי] Cocabi itself can also mean Cocabene, that is, born at Cocaba? There are several towns of this name in Syria and Arabia. One is in Basanitis, of which Epiphanius speaks in the Nazaraeans, writing that their sect flourished ἐν τῇ Βασανίτιδι τῇ λεγομένῃ Κωκάβῃ, Κωχάβῃ δὲ Ἑβραϊςί [en tē Basanitidi tē legomenē Kōkabē, Kōchabē de Hebraisti]. And in the Ebionites: Ἄρχεται μὲν τὴν κατοίκησιν ἔχειν ἐν Κωκάβῃ τινὶ κώμῃ ἐπὶ τὰ μέρη τῆς Καρναΐμ, Ἀρνὲμ, καὶ Ἀςαρὼθ ἐν τῇ Βασανίτιδι χώρᾳ [Archetai men tēn katoikēsin echein en Kōkabē tini kōmē epi ta merē tēs Karnaim, Arnem, kai Astarōth en tē Basanitidi chōra]. And below: Ἀπὸ Μωαβίτιδός τε, καὶ Κωχάβων τῆς ἐν τῇ Βασανίτιδι, ἐπέκεινα Ἀδραῶν [Apo Mōabitidos te, kai Kōchabōn tēs en tē Basanitidi, epekeina Adraōn]. And in the Archontics, of Eutactus, the founder of the sect: Κατῴκησεν ἐν τῇ Ἀραβίᾳ ἐν Κωχάβῃ, ἔνθα αἱ τῶν Ἐβιωναίων τε καὶ Ναζωραίων ῥίζαι ἐνήρξαντο [Katōkēsen en tē Arabia en Kōchabē, entha hai tōn Ebiōnaiōn te kai Nazōraiōn rhizai enērxanto]. There are other Cochabeni, or Cauchabeni, in Arabia Deserta, of whom Ptolemy speaks, book 5, chapter 19: Κατέχουσι δὲ τῆς ἐρήμου ταύτης Ἀραβίας, τὰ μὲν παρὰ τὸν Εὐφράτην ποταμὸν Καυχαβηνοί [Katechousi de tēs erēmou tautēs Arabias, ta men para ton Euphratēn potamon Kauchabēnoi]. And a little after: Ὑπὸ μὲν τοῖς Καυχαβηνοῖς Αἰσῖται [Hypo men tois Kauchabēnois Aisitai]. There is also in the valley of Damascus the town كوكبا [Kawkabā] Caucaba, which the Nubian Geographer mentions, Clim. [=climate (section) of al-Idrīsī's geography, in the Latin Geographia Nubiensis] 3, section 5. And in Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī] كوكب [Kawkab] Caucab is a fortress of Tiberias, and كوكبان [Kawkabān] Caucaban one of Arabia Iemamitica. Some bird originating from such a place could therefore have been called כוכבי cocabi, or caucabi. Yet we conjecture something else, namely that כוכבי cocabi is the little owl, and that the Syriac translator here agrees with the Chaldees, for whom תנשמת thinsemeth is אותיא, otus, or בותא, eagle owl, birds very like the little owl. This [III, 33] conjecture of ours rests on the following reasons. Little owls are said to cucubare [hoot]. The author of the Philomela:
“The light-shunning little owl hoots in the darkness.”

And Aristophanes in the Birds expresses the song of little owls by the doubled sound κικκαβαῦ, κικκαβαῦ [kikkabau, kikkabau]. And the birds themselves are called κικκαβαὶ [kikkabai], as the Scholiast has there: Κικκαβαῦ) τὰς γλαῦκας οὕτω φωνεῖν λέγουσιν, ὅθεν καὶ κικκαβὰς αὐτὰς λέγουσιν [Kikkabau) tas glaukas houtō phōnein legousin, hothen kai kikkabas autas legousin]. Others prefer κοκκοβὰς [kokkobas]. Hesychius: κοκκοβάρη· γλαύξ [kokkobarē; glaux]. Read instead: Κοκκοβά· ἡ γλαύξ [Kokkoba; hē glaux]. It is also written Κουκουβὰ [Koukouba], whence κουκουβαΐαι [koukoubaiai], glauci fish, because they are of the same colour as τῇ γλαῦκι [tē glauki], that is, the little owl. The Scholiast of Oppian on line 170 of book 1 of the Halieutica: Γλαυκοί· αἱ κουκουβαΐαι [Glaukoi; hai koukoubaiai]. Hence it is very likely that the Syriac ܟܘܟܒܝ [כוכבי] cocabi here stands for the little owl ^{R3}. But I think that the Samaritan ࠒࠐࠅࠐࠄ [קפופה] kaphupha also belongs here, as does the Chaldee קפופא kephupha. So the two Chaldees, the Syriac and the Samaritan understand nearly the same thing by the Hebrew word תנשמת thinsemeth.

But the two Arabic versions have here شاهين [shāhīn] sahin, which Giggeius [=Antonio Giggei, Thesaurus linguae Arabicae (Milan 1632)] ineptly renders swan or porphyrio, since the sahin is a bird of prey and one of the τῶν γαμψωνύχων [tōn gampsōnychōn]. Of it Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt] says: طير معروف من جوارح [col. 288] الطير عدو الحمام اذا راه الحمام يعتريه ما يعتري الشاه من الذيب والغار من الهر والحمام اسرع طيرانا منه الا انه اذا راه يضعف عن الطيران خوفا واذا راته السلحفاه ويعطيه ظهرها فلا يعمل منقار الشاهين فيها فيحملها الشاهين ويصعد بها نحو السما ويرميها علي حجر صلد لتنكسرت فياكلها واذا مرض الشاهين اكل الدراريج يزول مرضه [ṭayr maʿrūf min jawāriḥ al-ṭayr ʿadūw al-ḥamām idhā raʾāhu al-ḥamām yaʿtarīhi mā yaʿtarī al-shāh min al-dhīb wa-al-ghār min al-hirr wa-al-ḥamām asraʿ ṭayarānan minhu illā annahu idhā raʾāhu yaḍʿuf ʿan al-ṭayarān khawfan wa-idhā raʾathu al-sulaḥfāh wa-yuʿṭīhi ẓahrahā fa-lā yaʿmal minqār al-shāhīn fīhā fa-yaḥmiluhā al-shāhīn wa-yaṣʿad bihā naḥw al-samā wa-yarmīhā ʿalā ḥajar ṣald li-tankasirat fa-yaʾkuluhā wa-idhā mariḍa al-shāhīn akala al-darārīj yazūl maraḍuhu] “A well-known bird of the raptorial kind. It is a bird hostile to doves. When doves see the sahin, the same thing happens to them as to a sheep [III, 34] at the sight of a wolf, and to a mouse at the sight of a cat. For although the dove surpasses it in flight, yet when it sees it, it grows weak with fear. The tortoise turns its back to it, against which the beak of the sahin can do nothing; but the sahin seizes it, lifts it up to the heavens and throws it down onto a hard stone, so as to eat it once broken. When the sahin is sick, it is cured by eating cantharides.” And Damir, after explaining that in the plural one says شيواهين [shīwāhīn] saivvahin and شياهين [shiyāhīn] sajahin, that the word is in use among the Arabs although it is foreign, and that there are three kinds of it, 1. the sahin properly so called; 2. قطامي [quṭāmī] kotami, that is, greedy for flesh; 3. انيقي [anīqī] aniki, or, as another copy has it, اسقي [asqī] aski, describes the first kind thus: الشاهين في الحقيقه من جنس الصقر الا انه ابرد وايبس منه مزاجا ولاجل ذلك تكون حركته من العلو الي اسفل شديدة ولهذا ينقض علي صيده انقضاضا من غير تحويم وعنده جبن وفتور وهو مع ذلك شديد الضراوة علي الصيد ولاجل ذلك ربما ضرب بنفسه الارض ومات وعظامه صلب من عظام ساير الجوارح وبعضهم يقول الشاهين كاسمه يعني الميزان لانه لا يحتمل ادني حال من [col. 289] الشبع ولا ادني حال من الجوع المحمود من صفاته ان يكون عظيم الهامة واسع العينين رحب الصدر ممتلي الزور عريض الوسط غليظ ^{a)} الفخذين قصير الساعدين ^{b)} قليل الريش رقيق الذنب اذا صلب عليه جناحيه لم يفضل منه شي واذا كان كذلك صاد الكركي وغيره [al-shāhīn fī al-ḥaqīqa min jins al-ṣaqr illā annahu abrad wa-aybas minhu mizājan wa-li-ajl dhālika takūn ḥarakatuhu min al-ʿuluw ilā asfal shadīda wa-li-hādhā yanqaḍḍ ʿalā ṣaydihi inqiḍāḍan min ghayr taḥwīm wa-ʿindahu jubn wa-futūr wa-huwa maʿa dhālika shadīd al-ḍarāwa ʿalā al-ṣayd wa-li-ajl dhālika rubbamā ḍaraba bi-nafsihi al-arḍ wa-māta wa-ʿiẓāmuhu ṣulb min ʿiẓām sāyir al-jawāriḥ wa-baʿḍuhum yaqūl al-shāhīn ka-smihi yaʿnī al-mīzān li-annahu lā yaḥtamil adnā ḥāl min al-shibaʿ wa-lā adnā ḥāl min al-jūʿ al-maḥmūd min ṣifātihi an yakūn ʿaẓīm al-hāma wāsiʿ al-ʿaynayn raḥb al-ṣadr mumtaliʾ al-zawr ʿarīḍ al-wasaṭ ghalīẓ al-fakhdhayn qaṣīr al-sāʿidayn qalīl al-rīsh raqīq al-dhanab idhā ṣaluba ʿalayhi janāḥayhi lam yafḍul minhu shayʾ wa-idhā kāna ka-dhālika ṣāda al-kurkī wa-ghayrahu] “The true sahin is of the saker kind, except that it is of a colder and drier temperament, and hence its movement is most powerful from above downwards. That is why it descends upon its prey without any circling. And although it is sluggish and slack by nature, it is carried to the hunt with such force that it sometimes hurls itself headlong to the ground and dies. Yet it has harder bones than any other bird of prey. Some assert that the name sahin means balance, because this bird cannot bear the slightest hunger nor the slightest satiety. The most highly prized of this kind is the one with a large head, wide eyes, a broad chest, a full upper breast, a broad middle, thick thighs, short arms (var. legs), few feathers and a slender tail. If along with these marks it has strong wings, nothing will be more excellent, and it will hunt cranes and other birds of that sort.” He goes on to say that this kind of hawking [III, 35] first originated with Constantine, emperor of the Romans, who had الشواهين [al-shawāhīn] sahins trained to fly above his head and to give him shade, so that he would not be scorched by the heat of the sun. I also have in my possession a French book entitled Conference des fauconniers, that is, Conference of Falconers. In it, in the tenth conference, the sahins are described thus: “The sahins are falcons of high rank, which have a head flat on top and plumage edged with white and also evenly marked with russet. Hence it seems that nature has placed on their head a garland or crown, as a mark of their excellence. In short, these are the falcons which were formerly called peregrines, or Tartar falcons, although this was improperly said” ^{R4}. And the most distinguished Thuanus, after saying that it is called Peregrine because its origins are uncertain, describes it thus in book 1 of On Falconry, page 14:

— — a large head, a lofty neck, a flattened crown: from here a white line runs crosswise along each temple and meets, and crowns the broad top, and, with the neck bent back, at length branches off into several strands, girding the neck with an artful chain. The body is not so huge; but it has a long thigh and slender wings, short legs, and a short tail guides its swift efforts against the opposing air.
See the rest there, and you will find that it agrees with the description of the Arabs.

The Hebrews also play their part here, and on this word R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] says: היא קל״בא שו״ריץ ודומה לעכבר הפורח בלילה, "in French it is called calve-souris (chauve-souris, that is, bat), which resembles a mouse and flies by night." Yet [III, 36] Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] in his Lexicon writes: כתב רש״י ז״ל כי הוא הנקרא צ״ואיטא, "R. Selomo Jarchi [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac), called Jarchi by the Christian Hebraists] of blessed memory wrote that it is the animal which in French is called chovette, that is, the little [col. 290] owl." However that may be, the most learned of the Hebrews, Baal Hatturim [=Jacob ben Asher (d. 1343), commentary on the Torah], Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra], Kimchi etc., hold that it is a bird so called because כל רואה אותה ישום, whoever sees it wonders and is astonished. This must be properly understood. For to wonder or to be astonished is שמם, and the form of the noun does not allow תנשמת thinsemeth to be derived from it, since it plainly belongs to נשם nasam. But in that language it can happen that the same word has two origins, one with respect to its form, the other with respect to its meaning. And you will find not a few words which take their form from the defective Pe-Nun verbs, such as נשם nasam, but their meaning from the verbs doubling the second radical, such as שמם samam. Thus נחילות nechiloth, a kind of pipe, Ps 5:1, has its form from the verb נחל nachal, to possess, but its meaning from the verb חלל chalal, to pierce, whence also חליל chalil is a pipe, Isa 5:12, and חללים chalalim, that is, pipes, Jer 48:36. And the word נכסים necasim, that is, riches, is by the same reasoning derived from כסס casas, that is, to count. And נארים nearim, that is, the accursed, Ps 89:10, though as if from נאר, has its meaning from ארר arar, that is, to curse. And in Isa 22:7 the words המסכה הנסוכה, the veil drawn over, and in Isa 30:1. ולנסוך מסכה, and to draw a veil over, although derived from the verb נסך nasach, which is to pour, nevertheless borrow their meaning from the verb סכך sachach, which is to cover and to draw over. And in Lev 24:11 16. you will find נקב nakab, i.e. to pierce, used three times for קבב kabab, i.e. to curse. But, not to seek examples further afield: like תנשמת thinsemeth, so also נשמה nesama, properly the rational soul, comes in respect of form from the root נשם nasam, but in respect of meaning they would derive it from the word שמים samajim, which means the heavens; because
Fiery is its vigour, and heavenly its origin.

Kimchi in his Lexicon: לא מצאנו נשמה חוץ מנשמת האדם ורבים אמרו שנקראת כן בעבור שהיא מן השמים ואם הם שנים שרשים נמצאו כמוהו רבים, "We do not find the word nesama except of the human soul, which many assert is so called because it comes from the heavens; and, though there be two roots, many words of this kind are found." From these examples, then, it is clear that the word תנשמת thinsemeth too can be traced back to the verb שמם samam (which means to wonder and to be struck with astonishment), as we have shown is affirmed by the most learned of the Hebrews. Granting this, it will be highly probable that תנשמת is the little owl, at whose unusual form the other birds are astonished. Timon the writer of Silloi, in Laërtius and Hesychius Illustris, on Arcesilaus:
Οἱ δέ μιν ἤυτε γλαῦκα πέριξ σπίζαι τερατεῦντο, [Hoi de min ēute glauka perix spizai terateunto,]

But they marveled at him like the little birds that surround the little owl. Lucian in the Harmonides: Ἔνθα ἂν καὶ νῦν φανῇς, συνδέουσιν ἐπί σε πάντες, ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τὴν [III, 37] γλαῦκα τὰ ὄρνεα [entha an kai nyn phanēs, syndeousin epi se pantes, hōsper epi tēn glauka ta ornea]; Wherever you are seen, all run together to you, as other birds to the little owl. Dio Chrysostom says the same of it in the Olympic oration, right at the beginning: Ἐκείνην περιέπουσι τὰ ἄλλα ὄρνεα, ὅταν δὲ ἴδῃ μόνον, τὰ μὲν καθιζόμενα ἐγγὺς, τὰ δὲ κύκλῳ περιπετόμενα [ekeinēn periepousi ta alla ornea, hotan de idē monon, ta men kathizomena engys, ta de kyklō peripetomena], etc. Οἱ δὲ ἄνθρωποί φασιν, ὅτι θαυμάζει τὴν γλαῦκα τὰ ὄρνεα [hoi de anthrōpoi phasin, hoti thaumazei tēn glauka ta ornea]; The other birds follow her, and when they merely see her, some sit down near her, others fly round her in a circle, etc. And men say that the birds marvel at the little owl. The makers of fables invent another reason, namely that the birds marvel at her and are stupefied at the sight of her because of a horrible crime she once committed. Servius on the first book of the Georgics: Nyctimene, after she had lain with her father and recognized the crime, hid herself in the woods and fled the light, where by the will of the gods she was changed into a bird (the little owl), which, because of so great a crime, is an object of wonder to all birds. On Nyctimene see more in the second book of Ovid's Metamorphoses, and in Hyginus, Fables 204 and 253. However fabulous these things may be, it is nonetheless established that the other birds are stupefied when they see the little owl, and, held fast by that stupor, are caught. Aristotle, History, book 9, chapter 1: Τὰ ἄλλα ὀρνίθια τὴν γλαῦκα περιπέτεται, ὃ καλεῖται θαυμάζειν· καὶ προσπετόμενα τίλλουσι. διὸ οἱ ὀρνιθο- [col. 291] θῆραι θηρεύουσιν αὐτῇ παντοδαπὰ ὀρνίθια [ta alla ornithia tēn glauka peripetetai, ho kaleitai thaumazein; kai prospetomena tillousi. dio hoi ornithothērai thēreuousin autē pantodapa ornithia]; The other little birds fly around the little owl, which is called marveling; and flying at her they pluck at her. For this reason fowlers use her to catch little birds of every kind. Hence Aelian, History of Animals, book 1, chapter 29: Αἱμύλον ζῶον, καὶ ἐοικὸς ταῖς φαρμακίσιν ἡ γλαύξ [haimylon zōon, kai eoikos tais pharmakisin hē glaux]; The little owl is a wily animal, and like sorceresses. And after explaining that it is carried about by fowlers to serve them as a decoy: Νύκτωρ μὲν αὐτοῖς ἀγρυπνεῖ, καὶ τῇ φωνῇ, οἱονεί τινι ἐπαοιδῇ γοητείας ὑπεσπαρμένη, αἱμύλου τε, καὶ θελκτικῆς, τοὺς ὄρνιθας ἕλκει, καὶ καθίζει πλησίον ἑαυτῆς· ἤδη δὲ καὶ ἐν ἡμέρᾳ θήρατρα ἕτερα τοῖς ὄρνισι προσήει [nyktōr men autois agrypnei, kai tē phōnē, hoionei tini epaoidē goēteias hypesparmenē, haimylou te, kai thelktikēs, tous ornithas helkei, kai kathizei plēsion heautēs; ēdē de kai en hēmera thēratra hetera tois ornisi prosēei] (read προσφέρει [prospherei]) μωκωμένη, καὶ ἄλλοτε ἄλλην ἰδέαν προσώπου στρέφουσα, ἐφ᾽ ὧν αἱροῦνται, καὶ περιμένουσιν οἱ νέοι πάντες ὄρνιθες, ἠρημένοι δέει [mōkōmenē, kai allote allēn idean prosōpou strephousa, eph᾽ hōn hairountai, kai perimenousin hoi neoi pantes ornithes, ērēmenoi deei] (read θέᾳ [thea]) καὶ μοίλᾳ γε [kai moila ge] (read αἱμυλίᾳ γε [haimylia ge]) ἰσχυρῶς, ἐξ ὧν ἐκείνη μορφάζει [ischyrōs, ex hōn ekeinē morphazei]; By night she keeps watch for them, and with her voice, as with a kind of magic song, coaxing and alluring, secretly scattered abroad, she draws the birds and makes them sit beside her. By day she offers the birds other enticements, mocking them and turning her face into one shape after another, by which all the younger little birds are caught and held, detained by the spectacle and the enticements of the forms into which she transforms herself. Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)], chapter 21 On Animals:

Αἱμύλιον ἡ γλαὺξ ἡ φιλέσπερος φύσει. Σκοπεῖν γὰρ εἰκὸς τῆς πανούργου τὸν δόλον. Μωκωμένη τὰς ὄρνις ἡμέρας ὅλης, Καὶ ποικίλη στρέφουσα μορφῇ τὴν θέαν, Σαίνει τὰ μικρὰ τῶν ὑποπτέρων γένη. [Haimylion hē glaux hē philesperos physei. Skopein gar eikos tēs panourgou ton dolon. Mōkōmenē tas ornis hēmeras holēs, Kai poikilē strephousa morphē tēn thean, Sainei ta mikra tōn hypopterōn genē.]

[III, 38] The evening-loving little owl is of a wily nature. It is worth observing her tricks. Mocking the birds the whole day, and displaying herself to be looked at in various forms, she fawns upon the smaller winged creatures. Palladius, book 10, chapter 12: Now (in the month of September) the fowling with the little owl is prepared in the snares, together with the other instruments of capture, so that it may be practised around the Calends of October. Petrus Crescentiensis, On Plants and Animals, book 10, chapter 16, which is On the gimo and the gimetta, that is, the male and female little owl: The other birds marvel at them and long to see them, as something new and unusual. For this reason men, seeing the other birds flying around the gimo and gimetta and gazing at them with the greatest eagerness, devised a new method of fowling: namely, by setting out these birds as a spectacle, to catch for themselves the others thus lured, with birdlime or nets. Rightly, then, is the little owl called תנשמת thinsemeth, as being astounding and wonderful, that is, to those little birds which, struck with stupor, it draws to itself. Accordingly not only the Hebrews, but among our own scholars Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)], Schindler etc. render it "little owl". And the two Chaldee versions, the Syriac and the Samaritan follow the same. As a corollary I may add a not unpleasing little fable about the ugliness of the little owl, taken from the Iambics of Gregory of Nazianzus, Poem 22:

Τὴν γλαῦκ᾽ ἐπέσκωπτέ τις· ἡ δ᾽ ἐφύγγανε Τῶν σκομμάτων ἕκαστον εὐστόχῳ λόγῳ. Ὅσσον κάρηνον! Τοῦ Διὸς δὲ πήλικον. Ἡ γλαυκότης δέ! Τοῦτο τῆς Γλαυκώπιδος· Φθέγγῃ δύσηχον. Ἡ δὲ κίττα καὶ πλέον· Τὸ λεπτοποῦν πῶς; Ψὴρ δὲ σοί τι φαίνεται; Ἐπεὶ δὲ πάντα ῥαδίως διέδρασε Ἑνὶ κρατεῖται, καὶ σοφή περ οὖσ᾽ ὅμως. Ἀλλ᾽, ὡς σοφὴ, σκόπησον· ὡς τούτων μὲν ἓν Ἑνὶ πρόεστι, σοὶ δ᾽ ἅπαντα καὶ λίαν· Γλαυκὴ, δύσηχος, λεπτόπους, βαρύκρανος. Τούτοις ἀπῆλθεν ἐντραπεῖσ᾽ ἡ φιλτάτη. [Tēn glauk᾽ episkōpte tis; hē d᾽ ephyngane Tōn skommatōn hekaston eustochō logō. Hosson karēnon! Tou Dios de pēlikon. Hē glaukotēs de! Touto tēs Glaukōpidos; Phthengē dysēchon. Hē de kitta kai pleon; To leptopoun pōs? Psēr de soi ti phainetai? Epei de panta rhadiōs dierdrase Heni krateitai, kai sophē per ous᾽ homōs. All᾽, hōs sophē, skopēson; hōs toutōn men hen Heni proesti, soi d᾽ hapanta kai lian; Glaukē, dysēchos, leptopous, barykranos. Toutois apēlthen entrapeis᾽ hē philtatē.]

Someone was mocking the little owl. She, however, parried each of the jibes with clever speech. Obj. What a head! Resp. But what sort of head does Jupiter have? Obj. And the grey-blue colour? Resp. This is proper to Minerva, the goddess with grey-blue eyes. Obj. You sing unpleasantly. Resp. The magpie sings even more unpleasantly. Obj. How (supply will it be excused) the thinness of your foot? Resp. What do you think of the starling? But after she had easily refuted everything, she was beaten on one point, however wise she was. Obj. But, as a wise one, take note: each of these is found singly in each of them, but in you all of them together, and beyond measure; for you are grey-blue, and crude in song, and thin of foot [col. 292] [III, 39], and heavy of head. At these words the good little owl went away, covered with shame ^{R5}.

notes.text: On this bird see Aelian, Hist. Animal. book 3, ch. 42; Pliny, Hist. Nat. book 10, ch. 46. It is the Fulica porphyrio of Linnaeus (vol. 1, part 2, p. 699, ed. Gmelin [=J. F. Gmelin, 13th edition of Linnaeus, Systema naturae (1788–93)]), with red forehead, many bracelets, a green body violet beneath; in French Poul-Sultane. To Oedmann [=Samuel Ödmann, Vermischte Sammlungen aus der Naturkunde] the πορφυριων [porphyriōn] of the Greeks seems to be the Phoenicopterus ruber of Linnaeus (vol. 1, part 2, p. 612) (Vermischte Sammlungen, 3, p. 57), but he does not add reasons for his opinion.

notes.text: Otus of Linnaeus: an owl with ear-tufts of six feathers, vol. 1, part 2, p. 288.

notes.text: Bochart's conjecture is confirmed by the testimony of Bar Bahlul, the Syro-Arabic lexicographer, who, as Castell [=Edmund Castell, Lexicon heptaglotton (London 1669)] reports in the Heptaglot, renders the Syriac ܟܘܟܒܝ [כוכבי] by the Arabic البوم الطيطي [al-būm al-ṭīṭī]. The first of these words means little owl, as we saw in the preceding Chapter; the second, which I could find in no lexicon, I interpret as spotted, from the Chaldee טִיט, so that a spotted little owl is meant. There are indeed several species of little owl marked with white or ash-grey spots.
notes.label: R3

notes.text: What Russell [=Alexander Russell, The Natural History of Aleppo (1756)] has about the شاهين [shāhīn] in the Natural History of the city of Aleppo p. 68 deserves to be added here: „For bird-hawking, they use a large falcon, with long legs, somewhat like the goshawk, which they call espeer; and two smaller falcons, stiled the one Zanous, and the other shaheen. This latter must be taken out of the nest, for when old they cannot be trained, and is so fierce, that it will fly at ang thing. If there were not several gentlemen now in England, who can attest it, I should scarce ventnre to mention, that with the shaheen, which is about the size of a pigeon, they often take the largest eagles, of which in this country there are plenty. They formerly were trained to seize the eagle under the wing: and so depriving him of the use of that part, they fell to the ground together: but their present method, as I am informed, is to seize him on the back between the two wings, which has the same effect, but brings him down more slowly, and so gives the falconer time, to come in to his hawk's assistance; in which if he is not very expeditious, the hawk is in either case speedily destroyed.“
notes.label: R4

notes.text: But J. D. Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], in Supplemm. ad Lexx. [=J. D. Michaelis, Supplementa ad lexica Hebraica] vol. 5, p. 1692, thinks it probable that the little owl, if it is indeed the Hebrew תנשמת, took its name from breathing, since certain species of little owls are accustomed at some season of the year to draw mournful breaths and gasps from deep in the chest. Yet Michaelis leans more towards the opinion he put forward in the hundredth Question proposed to those about to travel to Arabia by order of the King of Denmark, p. 328, that תנשמת is the goose, to which he thinks the name was given from נשם, breathing, because this bird, when angry, stretches out its neck and hisses at whatever it takes for an enemy. To the objection someone might raise, that the Jews do not count the goose among the unclean birds, he tries to reply that the traditions of the Jews about the meaning of Hebrew words deserve no credence, and that they permit many things contrary to the Law and have accepted them in daily use. According to the spirit of the Mosaic law on unclean foods, he says, the eating of no animal, not even the pig, should have been forbidden more than that of the goose, which is very unwholesome and especially fosters skin diseases. He said more in Mosaic Law vol. 4, §. 203, pp. 198—200, and §. 205, pp. 214–215. — To Oedmann (in the Vermischt. Sammlung, part 3, ch. 5, p. 50 ff.) תנשמת is the Pelecanus Onocrotalus of Linnaeus (vol. 1, part 2, p. 569), to which he thinks the name was given from breathing no less than to the lizard chameleon (see above, vol. 2, p. 505 of our edition). For just as this lizard swells up by drawing in air, so in the Pelecanus onocrotalus too the very large, capacious and wrinkled pouch that hangs beneath the lower mandible is easily dilated by breathing, so that its capacity is astonishing. To this argument, drawn from etymology, Oedmann added another (p. 52 ff.): that it is scarcely credible that Moses should have passed over in silence, in the food laws, a bird so common in Egypt and Eretz Yisrael, and not forbidden it to the tables of the Jews, since the bird is a voracious eater of fish and has tough flesh with an almost unbearable smell, especially when older. — You see, reader, that all these opinions, like Bochart's own, rest on etymologies; among them, however, Oedmann's seems to me more probable than the rest. But nobody could easily say anything certain about the bird תנשמת, since nothing but its name occurs in the sacred Codex.
notes.label: R5
